| 400 /s | 5.0 s            | 2.7 s | 8.4 s            | 4.7 s  | 4.6 s         | 2.0 s |
| 600 /s | 12.2 s           | 7.1 s | 16.2 s           | 10.6 s | 11.3 s        | 5.3 s |

Below saturation nothing moves: at 200/s, 42 ms and 62 ms before and after.

Checked by replaying 8 seeds of random writes and comparing 36 live function values and 80
lists with what a new reader finds: no difference, and a broken check is seen on 35 of 36.

Known limit: the viewer's own reads, those that built its caller, still test the whole
batch. They were absent from the measure, and did not cost anything worth a line.

## D-261: A flush reads the rows it expects together

Choice: amends D-258. Nothing changes for a developer.

D-258 gave each read the rows that lead to its pin, and each read then loaded its own: a
flush that used to read a batch in one statement read it in one statement per viewer, by
id, about 8 500 of the 23 113 statements of ten seconds of presence at 500 writes a second.

1. The walk of a flush says which rows will be asked for: those written, and the roots
   they reached. The first read that misses a row of a model reads those of that model
   with it.
2. A root with no connected reader is read for nothing: one more id in one statement,
   against one statement per reader.
3. Past 10 000 rows (the most a flush's shared reads hold), only what is asked is read.

## D-262: A live read names its viewer only where a rule says more

Choice: amends D-195 and D-259. Nothing changes for a developer.

A rule usually repeats its parent's on the way down: a chat shows to its members, and so
does a chat's member, by `{ chat: { is: <the chat's rule> } }`. Every viewer's read of a
chat so named that viewer in each of its relations, and read alone: 16 410 of the 26 442
statements of ten seconds of presence at 1 000 writes a second, 69 seconds of database time
out of 120.

1. A planned live read drops a relation's condition on the row above when that row's rule
   already holds it: the row shows only if it passes, and the relation's key on the target
   is what leads there. A condition asking anything more stays, whole.
2. A read naming nobody once that is done is one statement for all its viewers, each given
   the rows its rights let through (D-259). It also brings the roots the flush expects
   (D-261), at most 1 000 per statement: the next root asked for reads the next ones.
3. A read still naming its viewer, or counting a relation, reads only the rows it asks for:
   bringing the others along would cost each viewer every root of the flush.
4. Only live reads do this. Other reads could too, and it would simplify their SQL; that is
   a separate choice, to measure with `bench/compare`.

## D-263: A flush reads the rows related to its rows together

Choice: amends D-255. Nothing changes for a developer.

A rule walking a relation read only the related rows of the viewer who asked, so one read
per campaign: 5 977 reads of a campaign and 5 977 of its members out of 21 962 statements in
ten seconds at 1 000 writes a second, every other viewer of the same flush asking the next.

1. A read of the rows a relation leads to brings those of every row of that model the flush
   has read, at most 1 000 ids, for the first viewer to miss one. A viewer finding its own
   read costs no scan.
2. Past the 10 000 rows one read holds, the rows read together are too many to tell apart:
   the viewers already waiting go to a query, as they do for one crowded row (D-255), and
   each next viewer reads its own for the rest of the flush.
3. A row read is kept whole, so later viewers get it without waiting a turn.

Campaign at 1 000 writes a second: told p50 from 2 017 to 47 ms, and it holds; 1 958 to
1 052 statements a second.

## D-264: A composed statement is prepared once per connection

Amended by D-274, D-293, D-325.

Choice: amends D-47. Nothing changes in a developer's code.

Under load PostgreSQL spent more time planning the statements the adapter composes than
running them, and an application asks the same few, 72 to 200 in the benches.

1. A statement `text.ts` composes runs as a named statement, parsed once per connection. The
   raw SQL of `database.sql` (D-137) and the migrations stay unnamed: they may `select *`,
   which a change of table would refuse under a prepared statement. Every composed statement
   returns jsonb, booleans or counts, so a table changing replans it and nothing else.
2. PostgreSQL's `plan_cache_mode` stays on `auto`. Forcing a plan per run keeps nearly all the
   cost (chat at 600 writes a second: 492 done, commit p50 942 ms), so the gain is the plans
   reused. `auto` runs a statement five times with its values before it may reuse a plan.
3. At most 500 statements, a connection holding some 22 KB for each: a backend measured 2.1 MB
   before and 6 MB with 172 statements. A statement past 64 parameters, a long list of ids
   rarely asked twice alike, stays unnamed. Past the cap, new statements stay unnamed.
4. PgBouncer in transaction mode needs version 1.21 or later and `max_prepared_statements`
   above 0, or a statement finds itself unknown on another server connection. D-274 turns this
   off.

Composing also costs less. A write only composes its read and its checks when it has rows to
split, a name is put in snake case once, and a list's text allocates nothing per item:
`compileWrite` from 17.7 % to 10.4 % of the busy time in chat.

Told p50 and commit p50 in ms, 10 s per rate, with both:
chat at 500 writes a second 482, 207 to 52, 11; chat at 600 1 356, 1 072 to 267, 78, and it
holds, 498 to 591 done; campaign at 2 000 3 256, 2 648 to 2 098, 1 483, 1 316 to 1 491 done;
presence at 1 000 209, 16 to 88, 8. Alone, without the realtime: create 1.14 to 0.86, update
by id 1.20 to 0.89, a many disconnected and connected 1.58 to 1.06, read by id 0.96 to 0.79,
against the driver's 0.69.

## D-265: Subscribers of one row share its execution

Amended by D-267, D-272.

Choice: nothing changes in a developer's code.

On the real wire, graphql-js ran each live message once per subscriber and took 28.5 % of the
busy time: its executor makes an `AbortController` and, ending, a `DOMException` with its stack,
per message. That cannot be avoided from outside the library, so it now runs less often.

1. Subscribers of one row, with the same document, variables and master flag, share one
   execution within a turn of the loop. The key is that shape and the JSON of the row, so rows
   a rule or a virtual shows differently to two viewers run apart.
2. This holds because a generated resolver reads only its row, its selection and the master
   flag. `extend` (D-107) may add a resolver reading `context.caller`, so a schema `extend`
   changed runs per subscriber. An `extend` returning the schema it was given shares.
3. A live function's value runs per subscriber: it may be any object, with its own methods. A
   whole window does too, costly to compare and rarely sent to many at once.
4. The assumption is the one `Window.sent` makes (D-252): a row's JSON says what it shows. Only
   a plugin value hiding data from its JSON could differ, within one row of one model.
5. A result is forgotten as the loop turns, so no row stays longer than it takes to send.

Over GraphQL on a WebSocket, 1 000 subscribers of a window of 25, last message p50: an update
goes from 227.5 to about 165 ms, the author of 1 row in 50 from 210.2 to about 160, a new first
row from 172.6 to about 133. The subscribers' first windows do not change (3 386 to about
3 300 ms for 1 000 at once).

## D-266: Only messages above 1 KB are compressed

Amended by D-273.

Choice: nothing changes in a developer's code; sockets negotiate no context takeover.

D-154 compresses WebSocket messages above 1 KB, but `ws` honours its `threshold` only when the
negotiated extension has no context takeover. So every message was compressed, each going through
zlib's limited queue and the thread pool.

1. The server asks for `server_no_context_takeover` and `client_no_context_takeover`. A message
   below 1 KB goes out as it is.
2. The price: a message above 1 KB compresses alone, so it does not benefit from the ones before.
   Live messages are mostly small, and a big window has its own repetition.
3. Small frames now share a TCP chunk. `ws` on Node then delivers a refused growth's result and its
   end in one tick, and `graphql-ws` releases the socket twice if the link unsubscribes between
   them. So the link opens the next read and lets the refused one end by itself.

Over the wire, 10 000 users each following 20 others, told p50 and p95: 500 changes a second
6 297, 9 659 to 1 551, 2 382 ms; 1 000 a second 10 677, 14 201 to 4 045, 6 113 ms. 200 a second
62, 98 to 45, 73 ms. The memory does not move: 4.63 to 4.60 GiB, the clients' threads included.

## D-267: Subscribers of one row share it whatever window they follow

Choice: nothing changes in a developer's code.

D-265 shared an execution between subscribers with the same variables and the same root. Yet the
variables of a list usually differ, its `where` naming the viewer, and its root carried each
window's page info, read or not. So what users follow in common rarely ran together.

1. The shape holds only the variables read below the root field: its arguments chose the rows, and
   its resolver ignores them. A root's directives, its other selections and the fragments count,
   all of them whether used or not: a variable wrongly counted only costs a shared execution.
2. A message carries the page info only when the window's has moved; any other runs with a constant
   one, whose result is not sent. The count is the message's, or 0 likewise.
3. So windows sharing a row and a selection run once, unless their page info moved, and those whose
   page info did move still run apart. A real client selects `pageInfo` in about half of its lists.

Over the wire, 10 000 users each following 20 others, with D-266, told p50 and p95: 500 changes a
second 1 551, 2 382 to 593, 1 147 ms; 1 000 a second 4 045, 6 113 to 3 750, 5 683 ms; 200 a second
45, 73 to 41, 64 ms.

## D-268: A document is read and validated once

Choice: nothing changes in a developer's code.

An application sends the same few documents again and again, yet each subscription of each user
parsed and validated its own: a quarter of the retained heap was GraphQL syntax trees, about 10 KB
a subscription.

1. The GraphQL plugin keeps the 500 documents of at most 4 KB it was last asked for, over HTTP and
   WebSocket. A document that fails to parse is not kept. A document may hold user input in its text
   only if the client wrote it so; the bound is what such a client can make it hold.
2. A tree remembers the rule sets it passed. A document Master may send is still refused to a user
   past `maxDepth`, in either order. What fails validation is validated again.
3. Rule sets are built once per server, Master's and a user's.
4. Which subscribers run together is now stored by context, since their documents may be one.

Over the wire, 10 000 users, presence: connect 68.6 to 44.8 s, heap 1.52 to 1.10 GiB, told p50 at
500 changes a second 402 to 295 ms, at 1 000 a second 2 590 to 2 338 ms.

## D-269: A socket keeps a small compressor

Choice: nothing changes in a developer's code; the server negotiates a smaller window.

`ws` keeps a zlib compressor per socket from its first message above 1 KB, whatever the message
sizes after it. With zlib's defaults, a window of 15 bits and `memLevel` 8, it holds 109 KB a socket
after a 4.7 KB message and 243 KB after a 47 KB one, outside the heap, so that no heap figure shows
it: 1.1 to 2.4 GiB at 10 000 users.

1. The server answers `server_max_window_bits=12` and compresses with `memLevel` 5. RFC 7692 lets a
   server say so even to a client that did not offer it, so that no client loses compression.
2. A message compresses alone since D-266, and JSON repeats its keys within a row: a window of 4 KB
   sees what a window of 32 KB sees until a message is very large. On the wire: 25 rows the same,
   100 rows +0.8 %, 1 000 rows +3 %.
3. The compression level stays zlib's default: level 3 saves a third of the compressing, which runs
   off the event loop, for 6 to 12 % more bytes.
4. The client's own window is left alone: `ws` then refuses a client that does not offer
   `client_max_window_bits`, which would lose compression.

Measured alone, server and clients in separate processes, 2 000 sockets: 109 to 44 KB a socket after
a 4.7 KB message, 243 to 64 KB after a 47 KB one. The time to send does not move.

## D-270: A big list reads a few parts at once

Choice: amends D-254, point 3; nothing changes in a developer's code.

A list of 50 000 rows read its window in 25 statements of 2 000 rows, one after the other. For
4 of the 7 seconds of its opening the process had nothing to do but wait for them, and each of
them filtered all 50 000 rows by the caller's rights.

1. The parts of a big read run at once, 4 statements in all across every big read of the process,
   first come first. Six of the pool's 10 connections stay free for writes, which D-254 asks for.
2. A pool of fewer connections is not known here: its writes queue behind these statements for
   as long as the statements take, about 135 ms each.
3. A part filters only its own rows.

Parts were already separate statements, so nothing is less consistent than it was.

`bench/realtime/wire.ts`, 50 000 rows: one alone 7 100 to 4 622 ms, all at once 7 000 to 4 462 ms,
another client's message 56 / 71 to 59 / 94 ms (median / worst). Twenty subscribers at once:
76.9 s, 126 s when D-254 measured them.

## D-271: A change after a quiet goes at once

Choice: amends D-154, which sent the changes within 50 ms as one message; nothing changes in a
developer's code.

Every change waited a fixed 50 ms before its flush, so 50 of the 84 ms a lone write took to reach
its readers over the wire were a timer with nothing to gather.

1. Two flushes stay at least 50 ms apart, what D-154 asked of the gather: the changes in between
   share one message.
2. A change more than 50 ms after the last flush starts one at once. Its transaction's other
   changes come with it, since notifications of one tick reach the engine together.
3. Writes outside a transaction may now make two messages rather than one: the first write alone,
   the others 50 ms later, no later than they came before. That costs a chat message of 4 writes
   13 statements instead of 10.
4. Under load a flush is always less than 50 ms old, so nothing changes.

`bench/realtime/platform-wire.ts`, 10 000 users, a lone chat message: 84 to 21-38 ms; a lone change
of presence: 84 to 25-36 ms, with presence at 1 000 /s where it was. Chat at
400 /s: told p50 59 to 52 ms, p95 189 to 167 ms. At 600 /s it holds 476 /s, 431 before.

## D-272: A big live window runs in parts

Choice: amends D-154 and D-265; nothing changes in a developer's code or on the wire.

graphql-js runs a selection without yielding: the first message of a live list of 50 000 rows held
the event loop for 1.8 s, and every other user of the server waited that long.

1. A window of more than 2 000 rows runs 2 000 rows at a time, about 40 ms each, with a turn of the
   loop between two parts. Page info and count are the whole window's, in every part, and each edge
   keeps its cursor.
2. Only the window sent whole does: what a change sends is a few rows.
3. A part with an error runs the window again whole, so that an error's path counts from the
   window. An error is rare, and a window's parts read rows they already hold.
4. Only where the generated resolvers run every field (D-265): a field given by `extend` may read
   the whole connection.
5. Sending the message stays one block of about 0.5 s at 50 000 rows, `JSON.stringify` inside
   `graphql-ws`; at the 20 000 rows of the default budget, about 0.2 s.

`bench/realtime/wire.ts`, 50 000 rows, 1 subscriber: longest stall 1 795 to 501 ms, opening 4.6 s
unchanged. With 20 subscribers: longest stall 1 812 to 632 ms, the others' longest wait 1 801 to
1 129 ms, all opened in 76.9 to 68.7 s.

## D-273: Only messages above 2 KB are compressed

Choice: amends D-154 and D-266; nothing changes in a developer's code, and a client sees a few more
bytes.

A message compresses alone since D-266, in zlib's limited queue and the thread pool, once for each
socket. A change of one row is the message that goes to the most sockets, and it is about 1.6 KB.

1. Messages up to 2 KB go out as they are; above, they compress as before.
2. The price, on a message of a few rows with a cursor: 1.2 KB goes out as 1.2 KB rather than 0.6,
   and 2 KB rather than about 0.8. A window of 25 rows still compresses.
3. 4 KB gains no more on a row's change and costs up to 2.6 KB a message, so it was not kept.

`bench/realtime/wire.ts`, 25 rows and 1 000 subscribers: an update 120 to 94-98 ms, the author of a
row in 50 112 to 86-88 ms. `platform-wire.ts`, 10 000 users, one run each: campaign at 1 500 asked
1 020 to 1 201 written a second, chat at 600 asked 454 to 478, connecting the chat 50.7 to 46.7 s and
the process 4.11 to 3.49 GiB, the clients' threads included: fewer sockets ever keep a compressor.

## D-274: `prepared: false` runs every statement unnamed

Choice: amends D-264. A developer's code changes only to turn it off.

D-264 prepares what the adapter composes, and a connection pooler that shares server connections
between clients may then find a statement unknown: PgBouncer in transaction mode before 1.21, or
without `max_prepared_statements`. Such an application had no way out but changing its pooler.

```ts
// Before: always prepared.
database: postgres({ url: process.env['DATABASE_URL'] })

// After: the same by default, and a way out.
database: postgres({ url: process.env['DATABASE_URL'], prepared: false })
```

1. `prepared` is a boolean on `postgres()`, `true` by default. `false` sends every statement as
   an unnamed one, the planning cost D-264 removed coming back with it.
2. It holds for one adapter, so two applications in a process choose apart. The list of statements
   stays shared: it costs nothing to a connection that never reads it.
3. No option on the cap or the planning: nothing has asked for one.

## D-275: `liveFetch` reconnects at a random moment of its wait

Choice: no developer's code changes. Clients cut together no longer come back together.

`liveFetch` waited exactly its backoff before reconnecting, 100 ms doubling to 5 s, so every client
cut by the same restart reconnected in the same instant. `graphql-ws` already adds randomness by
default, 300 ms to 3 s, and needs nothing.

1. The wait is `Math.random() * backoff`, full jitter: the whole wait is random, which spreads twice
   as far as keeping half of it fixed. The doubling is what protects a server that refuses, and
   stays.
2. The first wait and the 5 s cap do not change. A longer cap would spread further, at the price of
   the 10 s resume window (D-154).

This is not what absorbs a mass reconnection. The storm bench (`bench/realtime/README.md`,
2026-11-06) shows 9000 clients arriving within 5 s taking about as long as 9000 arriving at once on
one process, and no delay at 150 a second: what absorbs it is arriving slower than a process connects.

## D-276: The server's connection queue holds 4096

Choice: no developer's code changes, and no option. Connections arriving together wait instead of
being cut.

1. The HTTP server listens with `{ port, backlog: 4096 }`, a constant. The system caps it at its own
   limit: `net.core.somaxconn`, 4096 on a recent Linux, 128 on macOS.
2. Past the queue, what happens stays the system's: Linux cuts or ignores the attempt.

Why, from the storm bench (`bench/realtime/README.md`, 2026-11-06), Linux, one process, 9000
arriving within 5 s: Node's default of 511 lost 800 to 1500 attempts and took 124 to 140 s, retries
included. With 4096 it lost none and took 62 s. A bare Node server shows the same: 3500 connections
at once wait at most 1175 ms at 511, and at most 192 ms at 4096.

Rejected:

- An option: nothing tells a developer what else to set it to, and a higher value than the system's
  does nothing.
- Leaving it to a reverse proxy: most deployments have one, and it then meets the same queue.

## D-277: A few connections open at once

Amended by D-286.

Choice: no developer's code changes, and no option. Under a storm, those arriving wait their turn
in the server, and the writes of those already there go on.

1. A process runs at most 8 opening tasks at once, in the order they came: reading a connecting
   caller, planning and first reading a live read, and the first run of a live function. The gate
   is in the realtime engine, so GraphQL and SSE share it (D-129).
2. The others wait without holding a PostgreSQL connection, so they fail no 10 s wait for one
   (`postgres()`'s `wait`), and take nothing from a write or a request.
3. A turn is given back after 5 s even when its task still runs: a hanging `identify` or live
   function slows the openings and does not stop them.
4. A read whose connection closed while it waited reads nothing.
5. Not behind the gate: `fetchMore`, a resend, a flush and a rebuild (8 viewers at a time since
   D-154), HTTP requests, and a query over a socket. An HTTP storm can still meet the 10 s wait.

Why, from the same bench: 9000 arriving at the same instant queued thousands of reads in the pool,
and more than 10 s in the queue fails. That made about 10 600 first reads fail, and 207 of about
1500 writes of connected users. What an opening costs is the process's time, about 145 a second
whichever queue holds them, so holding them in the server costs nothing the pool's queue did not.

8 is what a flush already allows, and leaves connections to the writes in the default pool of 10.

Rejected:

- A public option: no measure says a value would suit better, and the pool's size is a developer's
  to change first.
- A larger pool: it moves the queue to PostgreSQL.
- Serving the most recent first: those who waited longest would wait for ever.

## D-278: A failure of the server closes a socket with `1013`

Choice: amends D-178, point 2. `4403` now means refused, and only that.

1. When the caller read is another user, or `identify` throws a `PublicError`, the socket closes
   with `4403`, as before.
2. When `identify` fails any other way, on connecting or later, or when a viewer fails, the socket
   closes with `1013` ("Try again later"). A query or a subscription sent to it meanwhile gets the
   same close, and its operation the error it had.
3. The viewer still closes: nothing runs as a caller that could not be read. The client that comes
   back is identified again.
4. SSE does not change: its stream ends without a code, and `liveFetch` reconnects.

Why: the same bench closed 1226 sockets with `4403` for no other reason than a busy pool. `4403`
says "you may not", which an application may read as "signed out". `graphql-ws` retries on both,
and treats `1011` as final, so `1013` is the code that retries and says what happened.

Rejected:

- Keeping the viewer open and reading the caller again later: it would keep following as a caller
  it could not read.
- `1011`: `graphql-ws` stops retrying on it, so a passing failure would end the client's connection
  for good.

Example, before: the pool is busy for a moment, and an application that treats a refusal as a
signing out signs its user out.

```ts
createClient({
	url,
	on: {
		closed: (event) => {
			if (Reflect.get(Object(event), 'code') === 4403) signOut()
		},
	},
})
```

After: the same code runs only for a real refusal. A busy pool closes with `1013`, and `graphql-ws`
reconnects by itself.

## D-279: `beforeCreate` sees the defaults in its types

Choice: in the `data` of `beforeCreate`, a field set by a default is not `undefined` in its type,
because `beforeCreate` runs after the defaults (D-67).

1. This holds for a fixed default, and for a function default that cannot return `undefined`.
2. A function default that may return `undefined` keeps its field possibly `undefined`
   (`DefaultFunction` allows it), so the type never claims what the run does not give.
3. An optional field with a default may still be `null`: a caller may write `null`, and the default
   takes only an absent value.
4. A list without a default stays possibly `undefined`: the implicit `[]` of a list is written after
   the hooks, so that a hook can tell that nothing was given.
5. Nothing changes at run time, and nothing changes for `beforeUpdate`, where no default runs.

Why: an application wrote `data.status ?? 'inProgress'` in a hook, repeating the model's default to
satisfy a type that was wrong about the order D-67 fixes. A repeated default drifts from the model.

Rejected:

- Typing every field of the draft as set: a required field without a default is left to a hook
  (D-67), and a list is only filled after it.
- A separate draft type per default kind in the public API: one conditional type states the rule, and
  applications never name it.

Example, before: the default is repeated.

```ts
const Quest = defineModel('Quest', {
	status: f.enumOf(['inProgress', 'done'], { default: 'inProgress' }),
	rank: f.number(),
}).with({
	hooks: {
		beforeCreate: ({ data }) => {
			data.rank = ranks[data.status ?? 'inProgress']
		},
	},
})
```

After: the model says it once.

```ts
beforeCreate: ({ data }) => {
	data.rank = ranks[data.status]
},
```

## D-280: A column added with a fixed default keeps it

Amended by D-358.

Choice: amends D-105 and D-120 point 3. A required field added with a fixed default takes it in the
rows the table held, and the column keeps it as its default.

1. No option: `sync` and `migrate create` both write one statement, with no `drop default` after it.
   The kernel still writes the value it validated (D-67), so the column's default serves only an
   insert that does not name the field, which is code still running without it.
2. A list without a default keeps `'{}'` in the same way.
3. A default the model later changes or removes stays as it was in the column: the snapshot does not
   hold column defaults, and only that same old code can reach it.
4. A change of the column's type drops its default in the same statement, since PostgreSQL may not
   convert it (`default for column cannot be cast automatically`). A type's change is therefore
   the moment a column stops keeping one.
5. A required field without a fixed default gets no column default, as it has no value to give: old
   code cannot insert during a deploy, and a migration says so with `tries` as before.
6. A list that takes an empty value only because the model gives it no default gets a comment in the
   `migrate create` file, below its statement, where the fill belongs. A `Statement`'s new `note`
   carries it; `sync` does not show it, since it says what to write in a file.

Why: dropping the default in the same transaction meant that during a rolling deploy, the old code's
creates failed with `not null` from the moment the migration ran. An application hand-wrote its
migration to work around that, and only the file's reader could know that the empty list of a new
field was a decision to take.

Rejected:

- An option on the field or the config to keep the default: the kept default costs nothing, and an
  option would ask every author a question that has one sensible answer.
- A second statement to drop the default before a retype: PostgreSQL takes both in one `alter`, and a
  plan reads better with one statement per change.
- Recording column defaults in the snapshot, to follow a changed default: every stored snapshot would
  change for a value only old code can reach.
- The comment above the statement: a fill written there would run before the column exists.

Example, before: `migrate create` wrote two statements, and old code failed on `not null`.

```sql
alter table "account" add column "languages" text[] not null default '{}'::text[];
alter table "account" alter column "languages" drop default;
```

After: old code still inserts, and the file says what to decide.

```sql
alter table "account" add column "languages" text[] not null default '{}'::text[];
-- The stored rows hold an empty "Account.languages": fill them here if the model needs a value.
```

## D-281: A list holds a minimum and a maximum of values

Amended by D-358.

Choice: completes D-120, D-127, D-242 and D-280.

1. A list takes `size: { min, max }`, as a `many` does:
   `languages: f.enumOf(Language, { list: true, size: { min: 1 } })`. Either bound may be left out;
   `min` defaults to 0, and `{}` or `{ min: 0 }` bounds nothing. Startup stops on the bounds D-242
   refuses, and on a `size` on a field that is no list (`Account.name: size bounds a list only.`).
2. The bound holds after the hooks, where a required field's check runs (D-67, D-88): a `before*` hook
   may fill or trim a list. A create that leaves a list out with `min` of 1 therefore passes
   validation and may be filled by `beforeCreate`, so the create input keeps the list optional.
3. The refusal is `VALIDATION_FAILED` on the field, for every caller, Master too:
   `{ path: ['languages'], message: 'Expected at least 1 value.' }`, or `Expected 1 to 10 values.`,
   `Expected at most 10 values.`, `Expected exactly 2 values.`. It is not `RELATION_SIZE`, as no other
   row's state decides it, and it is not the `TypeError` of a hook's bad element (D-88): a hook that
   leaves a list empty may be leaving what the caller sent.
4. It holds on what a write leaves, `push`, `pushUnique` and `remove` included (D-149): an update of
   a bounded list by an operation reads its row under its lock, as one of a field with a `validate`
   does, so that the kernel sees the result. An update that does not write the list checks nothing.
5. PostgreSQL enforces it as well, with a check of its own:
   `constraint "account_languages_size_check" check (cardinality("languages") >= 1)`, or
   `between 1 and 10`, or `<= 10`. It runs in the keys' phase, after any column it bounds and a fill
   written by hand. Adding it fails when a stored row holds another number of values, which the plan
   says with `tries`. The memory adapter holds no check: the kernel is its only guard.
6. D-280's kept `'{}'` default then fails that check, which is what is wanted: code still running
   without the field cannot insert a row breaking the bound, and fails on the check. A migration that
   needs old code to keep inserting adds the bound in a later deploy.
7. The GraphQL schema and the OpenAPI document state the bound in the field's description, after its
   own, as D-242 does: `Holds 1 to 10 values.`
8. A fixed `default` outside the bounds is not checked at startup: a create fails on it, with the
   message of point 3.

Why: a list that needs at least one value was a Zod `validate` on the field, which a hook's value
skips (D-67) and which only the kernel's writes run, with nothing in the database behind it. An
application that filled the list in a hook had to choose between validating the caller's value and
letting the hook fill it, and could not state the rule to its database without a hand-written check
that the next `migrate create` knew nothing of. `validate` still takes anything else about the values.

Rejected:

- A bound in `validate`, read from the Zod schema: Zod's own `.min(1)` lives inside a function the
  kernel cannot read, and it runs before the hooks.
- Refusing a list left out with `Required.`: it would need a second branch and a second wording for
  one rule. The message says what the list must hold.
- `minItems` and `maxItems` in OpenAPI: a `many` states its bound only in its description, and D-129
  keeps the transports equal. A client that needs them can ask.
- `size` on a field type's stored list: no use asks for it, and a field type's options are its own
  (D-122).

Example, before: a Zod rule the hook's value skips, and no check in the database.

```ts
languages: f.enumOf(Language, {
	list: true,
	validate: z.array(z.enum(Language.values)).min(1).readonly(),
}),
```

After: one rule, which holds for what the hooks leave, and in the database.

```ts
languages: f.enumOf(Language, { list: true, size: { min: 1 } }),
```

```sql
alter table "account" add constraint "account_languages_size_check" check (cardinality("languages") >= 1);
```

## D-282: A page shows what a developer writes

Choice: amends D-155. Readers find the documentation's facts, but its code shows too much: 240 of its 397 blocks
hold a line of test or harness, and a GraphQL request sits in a `graphql()` function no developer has.
Everything shown stays executed; what changes is which code is shown. It held first for a pilot on
`graphql` and `hooks`; its readers approved it on 2026-11-06, and it now holds for every page.

1. **A short test stays.** A region of a test is shown when it is 12 lines at most and calls neither
   `fetch` nor a function its test file declares. Its `expect` shows the result, and unlike a comment
   it is executed. A file of the starter is shown whole, whatever its length: a developer's project
   holds it as it is.
2. **A request and its response are files.** A GraphQL document is `requests/<name>.graphql`, a request
   with its HTTP grammar `requests/<name>.http`, and a response `requests/<name>.json`, each included
   whole. The example's test sends the file and compares the response with the JSON file, parsed.
   `scripts/requests.ts` does this for the tests. It is no public API, and no package holds it. A
   `.graphql` file starts with `query`, `mutation` or `subscription`, even where GraphQL lets a query
   omit it. Each message a subscription receives is a response file too: the test compares it as it
   arrives.
   What a command prints is `requests/<name>.console`: each `$ npx ultimabase …` line and its output,
   with the variables it sets, as a developer sees them in a terminal. The test runs each line and
   compares the output. A `bash` block in a page holds commands only. A migration a page shows is its
   real `.sql` file, included whole.
3. **What changes at each run reads `…`** in a response file. The test replaces the values of `id`,
   `cursor`, `startCursor`, `endCursor`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `correlationId`, `resume` and `remove`
   before comparing.
   A value the file must name, as an id in a REST path, is written `$id` in an `.http` file, as in
   GraphQL, and the test passes it.
4. **A long model is shown in pieces.** A region may be a fragment, as one hook of a `hooks` object. A
   page's first include still shows its file's imports, so a page may open with a small model of its
   own file.
5. **A page is written to be scanned.** It opens with one sentence and its shortest example, gives a
   section to each thing a developer wants to do, and moves edge cases into a `Details` part of lists
   and tables, above the reference. Nothing is folded away: search and reading stay whole.
6. **Tools hold it.** `scripts/docs.test.ts` holds, for each page: 60 words per paragraph, 25 lines per
   block, rule 1, and a sibling test naming each request file it includes.

The reference of each page and D-155's checks stay as they are: every exported value and option still
appears in an included region. Frozen versions are untouched. The landing page and the README (D-158)
show the same request files: an example or a copied block that names no region is its whole file.

Rejected:

- Never including a test: it needs a function around each snippet for no gain on a short block, and
  replaces an executed `expect` by a comment nothing checks.
- `toMatchFileSnapshot` for responses: it compares text, so it fights Prettier on the same file.
  Comparing parsed JSON leaves the file's layout to Prettier.
- Hiding lines of a region with a marker: a third kind of marker in `regions.ts` and in Fumadocs' own
  reader, where splitting a region needs none.
- Accordions for edge cases: they hide text from the eye and add a click, where a section at the
  bottom keeps the top short.
- Splitting `relations` now: a page that long needs its own decision once the pilot is judged.

Example, before: what a developer read to learn how to filter, around a function they do not have.

```ts
const body = await graphql(`
	{
		posts(where: { likes: { gte: 10 } }) {
			edges {
				node {
					title
				}
			}
		}
	}
`)
expect(body).toEqual({
	data: { posts: { edges: [{ node: { title: 'Notes' } }] } },
})
```

After: the document they send, then the response they get.

```graphql
{
	posts(where: { likes: { gte: 10 } }) {
		edges {
			node {
				title
			}
		}
	}
}
```

```json
{ "data": { "posts": { "edges": [{ "node": { "title": "Notes" } }] } } }
```

A short test stays as it is:

```ts
const ticket = await Ticket.create({ data: { title: '  Printer jam ' } }, as)
expect(ticket.title).toBe('Printer jam')
```

## D-283: A benchmark measures a whole request

Choice: amends D-100. Nothing changes in a developer's code.

`bench/writes` and `bench/compare` stop at the query, and `bench/realtime` at the socket of a
subscriber: nothing measured what a client's request costs, in the middlewares, the caller and the
transports. `bench/http` does, for REST and GraphQL, signed in and under a read rule, against a server
in production mode, with its clients in a process of their own. It compares the server's CPU per
request, beside the requests a second, and a bare `node:http` and `pg` as its floor. Details in
[`bench/http`](../bench/http/README.md).

## D-284: A response stays the adapter's light one

Choice: amends D-66. A developer's code does not change. Two headers change, listed below.

`@hono/node-server` answers without building a `Request` or a `Response`, and writes a JSON response
in one call, until something reads the body or copies the response. On every request, three middlewares
of `httpPlugin` did: Hono's `bodyLimit` opens the body, on a `GET` too, Hono's `cors` sets its headers
before the route, which turns the route's response into a copy, and `c.header` after the route copies it
again, and a copy sends its body through a stream.

1. A header set after the route goes on the response itself, and on a copy only when that response keeps
   its headers, as `Response.redirect`'s.
2. CORS on a request that is not a preflight sets its headers once the route answered. Hono's `cors` still
   answers preflights.
3. The body limit lets `GET` and `HEAD` through, and compares a declared `Content-Length` with the limit
   without opening the body. A body that declares no length, or a chunked one, is counted by Hono's as
   before.

Two responses change. `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` goes out only with an allowed origin, as it
already did on a route's own `OPTIONS`; it meant nothing to a browser without one. A route's own `Vary` is
kept, `Accept, Origin`, where the middleware used to replace it, which could serve a cached answer for the
wrong `Accept`.

The server's CPU per request, in µs, against the reference of `bench/http`, median of three runs, 5 s a
case; requests a second in brackets:

| Case                                     |     Before |      After |      |
| :--------------------------------------- | ---------: | ---------: | ---: |
| REST, read by id, a visitor              | 470 (2758) | 400 (3140) | -15% |
| REST, read by id, signed in              | 694 (1516) | 631 (1608) |  -9% |
| REST, a list of 25, nested, signed in    | 1186 (894) | 1118 (895) |  -6% |
| REST, create, signed in                  | 924 (1194) | 785 (1374) | -15% |
| REST, update, signed in                  | 1267 (846) | 1076 (863) | -15% |
| GraphQL, read by id, signed in           | 908 (1262) | 748 (1456) | -18% |
| GraphQL, a list of 25, nested, signed in | 1660 (510) | 1476 (497) | -11% |
| GraphQL, create, signed in               | 986 (1164) | 821 (1337) | -17% |
| GraphQL, update, signed in               | 1284 (824) | 1095 (885) | -15% |

## D-285: A read builds its rows as `json`, without numbering them

Status: agreed, 2026-11-06. No public API changes: what a read returns is the
same, keys and values alike.

The compiled read built each row with `jsonb_build_object` and its list with
`jsonb_agg(… order by "n")`, where `"n"` was a `row_number()` computed in the
subquery. `jsonb` parses every value into its binary form, sorts each object's
keys, and is then turned back into text for the client, which never uses any of
that; the numbering kept in memory, for the aggregate to sort again, what the
subquery had just sorted.

A read now builds `json` with `json_build_object` and `json_agg`, in the order
its subquery's `order by` gives. Only a list read backwards keeps `row_number()`,
to turn its rows round. A row of more than 50 fields keeps `jsonb_build_object`
for its chunks, since only `jsonb` has `||`, and embeds in the rest as a value.

The order rests on what PostgreSQL does, not on a sentence that promises it: its
documentation says of a sorted subquery that this "will usually work", and warns
only of an outer level that adds a join. Here the outer level is the aggregate
alone, a sorted subquery is never flattened, and `json_agg` has no combine
function, so it runs in one process above a `Gather Merge`, which keeps the
order. `read-json.postgres.test.ts` forces parallel plans and checks the order of
6000 rows, both ways and nested, on each server the suite runs on.

Measured on one connection, prepared, median in ms, the Docker round trip (0.57
ms) included, on 2000 posts for the first two rows, on 50 000 for the others, with
3 comments each:

| Statement            | Before |  After |
| -------------------- | -----: | -----: |
| by id                |  0.638 |  0.611 |
| a list of 25, nested |  2.084 |  1.684 |
| 1000 rows, flat      |   11.3 |    6.8 |
| 50 000 rows, flat    |  535.5 |  286.7 |
| 1000 rows, nested    |   36.2 |   22.0 |
| 50 000 rows, nested  | 1857.5 | 1006.9 |

The peak memory of the backend (`VmHWM`) falls from 146 MB to 73 MB on 50 000
flat rows and from 442 MB to 239 MB on 50 000 nested rows. The text sent grows
by about 3.5 %, the spaces `json_build_object` writes, already counted in the
times.

Over HTTP, `bench/http`, median of 3 runs, requests a second: a nested GraphQL
list of 25 rows from 497 to 742, a nested REST list from 895 to 1007. A live
list's first read, `bench/realtime/lists.ts`, subscribe time: 97.8 to 65.6 ms at
1000 rows, 2385 to 1733 ms at 50 000. `bench/compare`, 10 writers with their
novels and genres: 2.74 to 1.92 ms. Writes and reads by id do not change beyond
noise.

Rejected: keeping `jsonb` and only dropping the numbering, 7 to 10 % against 46 %
at 50 000 nested rows. The idea D-103 rejected, building a row straight from a
write's CTE, stays rejected: there is still one way to compile a read.

## D-286: Openings leave the event loop its turns

Amended by D-292.

Choice: amends D-277. No developer's code changes, and no option. A connection arriving during a
storm is accepted in a few seconds at most, and a new visitor or a health probe no longer waits
behind it, at the same pace of openings.

1. Node accepts one connection per turn of its event loop, so what makes a turn long makes every
   connection wait, in the kernel's queue. Openings now spend about 1 ms of a turn: past that they
   go on one a turn. A lone opening goes straight through.
2. They pass this point at the start of their task, and again once a list's first read is back,
   where its work begins.
3. Of the 8 opening tasks of D-277, a subscription of a connected client goes before reading the
   caller of a connection arriving, so that those there have all they asked before others begin.
   One turn of the gate in 8 goes to those arriving first: a flow of subscriptions cannot stop
   them. Among themselves each keeps the order it came in.

D-277's sentence "about 145 a second whichever queue holds them" holds for what an opening costs,
not for where it waits: in the kernel's queue it also holds up everything that is not an opening.
A bare `node:http` server doing 1 ms of work a request accepts 978 connections a second under
macOS, 961 under Linux, with 0.97 a turn, 200 and 198 at 5 ms. With 8 tasks a turn lasted about 7 ms,
hence the 145. Up to 4096 connections queued at that pace, about 28 s, with `/ready` behind them.

Measured with `bench/realtime/platform-wire.ts --storm`, 10 000 users, 9000 arriving, Linux, against
the commit before, in ms, p50 / p95 / max, in `bench/realtime/README.md`. All arriving at once: the
new visitor falls from 6827 / 26312 / 27903 to 4 / 3621 / 6028 and 4 / 1951 / 4724, all in stays at
58 s, and nothing fails. With PostgreSQL 2 ms away: 29 / 18106 / 20524 to 7 / 3168 / 5942, and from
61.7 s to 58.7 s. When arriving within 30 s: 14760 / 27489 / 33513 to 4 / 127 / 503.

What it costs. Within 30 s, the median of all a client's states rises from 15.3 to 18.3 s while the
longest falls from 34.1 to 31.8 s. Without a storm, 4000 users connect in 21.2 s instead of 20.5 s
and 1000 subscribers on one list in 2.8 s instead of 2.65 s: one turn more for each. In return, those
waiting while 100 clients open a list of 2000 rows wait 276 / 714 ms instead of 660 / 1781.

Rejected:

- Fewer openings at once. It looks free with PostgreSQL next to the process and is not: 2 at a time
  takes 136.5 s instead of 61.7 s with a database 2 ms away, 4 at a time 74.4 s, since a task spends
  its time waiting for the database, not working.
- A turn spending its budget of 2 ms, or running several at once: the new visitor's longest wait
  is 8.7 s against about 5 s, with no gain in the time all take.
- Pacing without the priority: accepting sooner mixes all clients' subscriptions in one queue, and
  the median of the first state rises by 30 %.
- Several listeners with `reusePort`: Linux only, and it hides `EADDRINUSE`. Threads cannot receive
  sockets in Node.

## D-287: A silent database is noticed

Amended by D-298, D-331.

Choice: no developer's code changes, and no option. When a network fails with no one told, such as
a failover moving the database's address or a firewall dropping a connection, realtime comes back
and waiting requests fail within about 20 s, instead of freezing with no sign until a restart.

1. The connection listening to the feed asks `select 1` every 10 s, and the answer has 10 s to
   come. Connecting and listening have the same 10 s.
2. Without an answer, the listener and every connection of the pool open before the question are
   cut, as a reset would. What they were running fails at once, with `PostgreSQL stopped answering.`,
   idle ones leave the pool, one held by a transaction goes when released. A warning says so.
3. The listener then connects again as after any loss, and the feed's `missed` tells what may have
   been lost.
4. The silence is judged after the sockets were read, one turn of the event loop after the deadline:
   a long turn delays the reading of an answer, and is not the database's silence.

A slow statement is left alone: the question goes through its own connection. A network gap of more
than 10 s now fails what was in flight, where it could have resumed; a shorter one changes nothing.
Cost: one `select 1` per process per 10 s.

Measured with an uncommitted fault bench, Linux, 8 readers, 2 writers and 50 subscribers, moving the
database to a new address at 15 s so that the old one goes silent. Before: reads stuck until the
bench's own limit of 120 s, no realtime message for the 225 s left, no warning, and a stop still
stuck after 20 s. After: all back 15 s after the fault, and a stop in 21 ms. PostgreSQL killed, its
connections terminated and a network cut of 20 s all recover too. A storm of 9000 arriving and an
overload of 2000 writes a second, with turns up to 529 ms, give no warning, and the storm's figures
are those of D-286.

The limit: the listener exists only when a plugin takes the feed. Without realtime, a statement in
flight on a vanished address waits for the operating system, about 15 minutes under Linux. Covering
it is a statement timeout on `postgres()`, a public option, which this decision does not add.

Rejected:

- `keepAlive` on the connections: it stays quiet while data awaits an acknowledgement, the pool
  already closes idle connections within 10 s, and a proxy answers it for a database that is gone.
- `query_timeout` of `pg`: its timer can fire before the socket was read, so a long turn would pass
  for silence, and the connection stays.
- Looking through `pg_stat_activity` on a new connection: heavier, and through a proxy it does not
  say which of ours are alive.
- A default statement timeout: it would end long queries that work today, a change of behaviour.

## D-288: A live list refills from the keys it holds

Choice: no developer's code changes. A live list's copy could stay wrong for good after concurrent
writes, with rows missing, out of order or `hasMore` false; it now always ends equal to a fresh read.

The window refilled with `cursor: { id: last }, skip: 1`. An adapter finds a cursor row's place from
what the database says now, and a database runs ahead of the flush that reads it: a write of another
process, or a `grow` during a burst, has not been told yet. So a window whose last row had moved read
from that row's new place and skipped what lay between, and one whose last row was deleted read
nothing and believed the list had ended. No later change repaired it.

1. A refill reads strictly after the sort keys the window holds for its last row, a filter of
   `afterKeys` in the adapter's own terms: past the key, or at it with the next key deciding, `null`
   where it sorts. Every adapter runs it, unchanged.
2. A row the window holds elsewhere is skipped, as the flush to come places it. So is a row this
   flush has just refused. When a page brings only such rows, the read goes on after it.
3. Each read is right but for writes after it, and each of those writes brings a later flush that
   reads the row again, so the window ends right.

The public `cursor` keeps its meaning: it names a row, and starts from where that row is.

Measured with an uncommitted script, on PostgreSQL 18: 2 processes, 4 writers each, lists opening,
growing and closing during the writes, 22 kinds of write under rules through relations, then 30 s
of quiet and a comparison of every copy with a fresh read as its caller. Before: 2 to 4 wrong copies
within the first three rounds of 5 s. After: none over 6 rounds on each seed.

Left as it is: under a script writing 700 times a second on a handful of rows, a flush can judge a
row refused while a page it just read brings it, because the flush's shared reads are older or the
right really changed. The list logs `it reads again`, reads whole and stays right.

Rejected:

- Having adapters resolve a vanished cursor: it fixes the deletion only, not the moved row.
- Reading the refused rows again without the flush's shared reads: the logs above stayed.

## D-289: A read from a cursor starts at its row

Choice: no developer's code changes. A page after a cursor no longer costs in proportion to its
place in the table, when an index serves its order.

`keyset` is an `or` over the sort keys, which PostgreSQL can only filter with: to read 100 rows at
99 % of 100 000, it walked the index from its start and threw away 99 000 rows. Paging through a
whole table was quadratic.

1. A read from a cursor adds `(a, b) >= (select a, b from t where <cursor> limit 1)`, `<=` for
   descending keys, which `keyset` already implies, so no result can change. A row gone gives
   `null`, so no rows, as today.
2. It takes the first sort keys that are plain required columns going one way, and stops at the
   first that is not. A first key that may be `null` gets no bound: `null`s sort outside any
   comparison, and an `or` for them would lose the index.
3. It is an uncorrelated subquery rather than the value `keyset` joins: PostgreSQL computes it once,
   as a constant for the index condition, and the walk keeps its order, in a nested list too.
4. `afterKeys` (D-288) gets no bound: a live list stays within its limit of 1000 rows by default.

Measured on PostgreSQL 18, 100 000 rows, pages of 100, `node` over the adapter, through every row:
order by `id` 25.8 s to 1.7 s, an indexed key and `id` 15.3 s to 1.7 s, descending 14.3 s to 1.7 s,
backwards 14.4 s to 1.7 s, under a filter 1.0 s to 0.18 s. A page at 99 % goes from 48 to 1.5 ms by
`id`. With no index, or an optional first key: unchanged, 206 ms a page. A first key of two values
with an index on all the keys: 38.4 to 0.23 ms for the statement. Filters rare, common, not indexed
or matching nothing, at 3 places in the table: no plan got worse, and the same rows.

Tests: every kind of key, ties, `null`s, a filter, forwards and backwards, nested, a row gone or
outside the filter, and the plan's index condition, on PostgreSQL 15 and 18. Without the bound, only
the 10 tests of the plan fail.

## D-290: A client's bad frame closes its socket, not the server

Choice: internal, nothing changes for a developer. A WebSocket that receives an invalid frame, or one past `maxPayload`, emits
`error`. `sockets.ts` listened to nothing on it, so the error went uncaught and
stopped the process: a client needed no account, only the origin check, and two
bytes, to stop a server with a realtime model. Every release since 0.1.0 has it.

The server's socket now listens to `error` and does nothing more. `ws` has
already closed that socket with the code for it (1002, 1007, 1009), and `close`
ends its subscriptions as for any other client.

Nothing is logged: the frame is the client's fault, it says nothing of the
server, and a log line would hand a stranger a way to fill the logs.

## D-291: A deploy waits for the schema's lock a try at a time

Choice: internal, nothing changes for a developer; amends how D-105 waits, not
how long, which still has no limit.

1. A sync or deploy takes the schema's advisory lock with
   `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock` or `pg_try_advisory_lock`, and tries again every
   100 ms, instead of one statement waiting for it.

Why:

- `create index concurrently` waits for every older snapshot to end, and it
  runs holding that lock. A statement waiting for the lock holds a snapshot: a
  cycle, which PostgreSQL ends by failing one of them.
- Several instances each running `migrate deploy` as they start is ordinary. 8
  at once with such a file: 7 failed with `deadlock detected`, each time. On 3
  million rows the index itself failed, for it builds past the others' only
  deadlock check: it stayed invalid, every deploy failed, and it took a
  `drop index` by hand. Between two tries a waiting transaction holds no
  snapshot, so the index no longer waits for it.

## D-292: A server on Linux listens on 16 sockets

Choice: internal, no option, nothing changes for a developer; amends D-286,
which turned this down, and D-276, whose queue each socket now has.

1. On Linux, outside a worker of `node:cluster`, a server opens 16 sockets on its
   port with `reusePort`, and hands what the 15 others accept to its one
   `node:http` server. Elsewhere it keeps one socket: `reusePort` is refused on
   macOS.
2. A port is first bound once without `reusePort`, then closed, so a port held
   by anything still gives `Port N is in use`.
3. A stop closes all 16 and waits for each, for the connections a socket accepted
   count on it alone.

Why:

- Node accepts one connection per turn of its event loop and per socket. A busy
  turn takes about 13 ms, so one socket lets in about 75 connections a second
  whatever the machine could serve, and clients with a connection go round again
  ahead of those without one.
- 2000 clients reading 100 rows, in Linux containers, for 20 s: at the end, the
  slowest wait 18 653 ms with one socket, 2337 and 2396 ms with 16, for the same
  throughput. The median rises from 107 ms to 2.3 s, since everyone now waits the
  same: with one socket, those let in went round quickly while about 500 others
  got nothing, past the patience of most clients. The worst `/health` goes from
  over 5000 ms to 422 and 913 ms.
- A storm of 9000 arrivals (D-286): a new visitor's p95 3621 and 1951 ms to 358
  and 325 ms, its worst 6028 and 4724 ms to 2370 and 2447 ms. All in 58.4 s to
  57.6 and 58.1 s. D-286 feared the first state's median would rise by 30 %, but
  the gate paces openings now: 30.7 s to 30.3 and 29.8 s.
- It costs nothing outside overload: 3094 against 3131 requests a second on the
  floor of the HTTP bench, median of 3.

What it does not do: past what the server can serve, requests that were queued
in the system now queue in the application. With 8000 new requests a second both
reach the 10 s wait for a PostgreSQL connection and answer 500, and the longest
stall of a turn is about the same (1296 ms, against 1406 and 1834 ms).

The check of a free port leaves a moment between it and the listening, so two
processes starting that same instant could share a port. Rejected: asking the
system whether anything holds the port, which is no less of a race and much more
code.

## D-293: A connection keeps the statements used last

Choice: a connection keeps prepared the 500 statements it used last, and a
statement takes room only once asked again. Before, the first 500 kept their
room until a restart, and anything after them ran unprepared. This amends point
3 of D-264 and changes nothing in a developer's code.

One visitor could use that up in 1.6 seconds with 500 public requests, each
filtering on another set of fields, and every later statement of the same
server then cost a planning. Medians in ms, PostgreSQL 18, one process, fresh
against after those 500 requests:

|                    | Fresh | After, before this | After, now |
| ------------------ | ----: | -----------------: | ---------: |
| Read by id         | 0.715 |              0.904 |      0.729 |
| List of 25, nested | 0.896 |              1.055 |      0.911 |
| Create             | 0.806 |              1.046 |      0.826 |
| Update             | 0.813 |              1.122 |      0.830 |

An application with more than 500 statements in real use met the same wall
without any visitor: whichever came first stayed.

1. Each connection keeps its own list, oldest first. Past 500 it has PostgreSQL
   forget the oldest with `deallocate`, and `pg` too, as `pg` otherwise keeps the
   text. A name is never reused: `pg` refuses a name with another text.
2. A statement runs prepared once it is asked again among the last 500 composed,
   counted for the process. Taking room at the first ask alone lost 15 % on a
   loop over 800 statements (4053 down to 3439 requests a second), as every ask
   then planned and spent a `deallocate`. With the second ask it holds 4058.
   Long lists past 64 parameters still stay unprepared.
3. Only what `pg` saw parsed is forgotten. A statement whose parsing failed in an
   aborted transaction does not exist, and forgetting it would abort the healthy
   transaction it happens in.
4. An aborted transaction refuses the `deallocate`. That statement then stays
   until the connection ends, which takes a transaction that has failed and has
   queries still running in it.
5. This reads the internal `connection.parsedStatements` of `pg`. Should `pg`
   rename it, statements stop being forgotten and the backend holds more, with
   nothing failing. The tests would catch it: they count the backend's list.

An attacker who sends each shape twice still takes room, but only for as long as
that room is the oldest. The statements in real use are used last, so they stay.
While 5 callers did that, a read by id took 1.20 ms against 1.22 ms before this,
and the attacker's own rate fell from 1300 to 1090 shapes a second for the extra
trip. The ordinary case does not move: read by id 0.72 ms, update 0.82 ms.

## D-294: A required text pins a live read

Choice: amends D-256's pins. Nothing changes for a developer: no option, no new
message, the same rows told.

A read with no id to lead to, whose filter requires a string or enum field to equal
a value or one of several (`where: { channel: 'x' }`, `{ owner: { in: [...] } }`), is
now pinned on that field. A write visits the reads of the value its row holds, not
every read of the model. The rules of D-256 apply as they stand: a write that moves
the field visits the whole shape, and so does a delete, whose row is gone.

An id or a relation still comes first, however far it is, since it names fewer rows.
Only the root's own fields pin: a text through a relation would make a write walk it
for little. `mode: 'insensitive'` pins nothing, since another spelling matches it, and
neither do numbers, dates and decimals, whose values are not compared as written.

Measured with 10 000 live reads held over SSE on one process, each on its own value,
median of 15 writes on a row none of them holds: told 65.9 to 74.5 ms before, 10.7 ms
after, against 10.7 ms with no read at all and 11.4 ms for reads pinned on a relation.

Costs: an update that does not move the field, of a row no list holds, now reads that
row, one statement a flush where there were none. A value that most reads share
visits them all, as before.

Known limit: a filter on several values through `OR` still pins nothing.

## D-295: The reads virtual fields make in one flush are shared

Choice: amends D-187. Nothing changes for a developer: `runMany` still runs once for
each subscriber, with its caller, and returns what it returns.

D-187 keeps each subscriber's value apart, since a rule may read the caller. That
stands. What is shared is the statement under it: during a flush, two reads asking
the same model with the same `where`, the rules already merged in, the same
selection and the same limits are one statement. A rule naming its viewer makes
another statement, so it never reaches another viewer. A read through a relation
carries the rule of the model it crosses, so that model's rule counts too.

1. It is safe in time: each read of a flush starts after the batch it follows
   committed, and flushes run one at a time. A write made after a shared read reaches
   a later batch, a later flush, and new shared reads.
2. Every reader gets its own copy of the rows and values, the first one included, so
   code changing what it read reaches nobody else.
3. A transaction or a write begun during a flush ends the sharing for that flush, so
   code reads what it wrote. A raw `database.sql` statement does not: code writing
   that way from a virtual field reads what was shared.
4. The flush's end ends it too: a promise a virtual field left running reads what is
   stored by then.
5. A failed read is sent again by the next one to ask.
6. It covers the reads of a live read that selects a virtual field, at any depth, and
   only within a flush: not the first read of a subscription, not a live function.
   Other live reads pay nothing; every other read pays one `AsyncLocalStorage` lookup.

Measured with `bench/realtime/virtuals.ts --rule-names-nobody`, 1000 subscribers on one
list, 10 writes creating a `Task`, statements and median to the last message:

| Window | Before               | After             |
| -----: | -------------------- | ----------------- |
|     25 | 1002 stmts, 422.8 ms | 3 stmts, 197.8 ms |
|   1000 | 1002 stmts, 6034 ms  | 3 stmts, 5130 ms  |

Cost: a rule naming its viewer gains nothing and pays the key and the copy, within
the noise: 423.1 to 439.7 ms at window 25, 6023 to 6200 ms at window 1000. What is
left at window 1000 is computing and comparing a million rows in JavaScript.

## D-296: An id's random part comes from `crypto.randomUUID`

Choice: `uuidv7` keeps its time and its counter (D-22) and takes its last 62
random bits from `crypto.randomUUID()`, which puts the same 62 bits at the same
place. Asking for 16 bytes per id, as it did, is a native call each time, where
Node draws a UUID from a block it keeps; and the text is written in one go. An
id takes 0.83 µs against 6 µs.
`createMany` of 5000 rows of six fields on PostgreSQL 18 takes 159 ms against
181 ms, median over three interleaved runs of each. A single `create` does not
notice: 5 µs of about 900.
Rejected: a block of random bytes of our own, the same thing with more code; a
faster, non-cryptographic source, since an id is not a secret but is hard to
guess today and a developer may have come to rely on it.

## D-297: A transaction's BEGIN does not wait for its answer

Choice: a transaction sends its first statement right behind `BEGIN`, in one
round trip. The pool opens its connections with `pg`'s `pipeline` option, and a
small dialect (`packages/postgres/src/begin.ts`) has `beginTransaction` return
once `BEGIN` is sent, keeping its answer for the COMMIT. PostgreSQL runs what it
receives in the order it came, so nothing changes for what a transaction sees or
writes, and each further statement still waits for the one before it.

1. A failing first statement behaves as before: the ROLLBACK follows, and the
   connection goes back clean. PostgreSQL answers each statement sent ahead,
   and `pg` knows which named statements it never parsed.
2. A `BEGIN` that fails is told at the COMMIT, or not at all when a statement
   failed first, since that statement's error is the cause worth telling. What
   can fail a `BEGIN` is a lost connection, which fails the statement behind it
   too.
3. A lost connection now fails the first statement rather than the `begin`.
   `pg` answers every statement it holds when its connection dies, so none
   waits forever.
4. `prepared: false` (D-274) keeps waiting for `BEGIN`, since a pooler may share
   connections, and nothing here was tried behind one.
5. The feed's listener keeps its plain connection: it runs no transaction.

`pg`'s `pipeline` is three months old as of this choice; it is pinned exactly,
and the first test of `begin.postgres.test.ts` fails if a new version of `pg` or
kysely sends in another order. A write under rules, an after hook or
`transaction()` gains a round trip; one statement alone never had a `BEGIN`.

Measured with `bench/writes`, statements unchanged, median in ms, two runs of each
on PostgreSQL next door (a 0.57 ms round trip) and one through a 2 ms proxy:

| Case                             | Next door, before |      After | 2 ms, before | After |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------: | ---------: | -----------: | ----: |
| update by id, a user under rules |        2.80, 2.79 | 2.41, 2.30 |        13.93 | 10.34 |
| delete by id, a user under rules |        2.63, 2.64 | 2.11, 2.11 |        13.60 | 10.14 |
| create, an afterCreate hook      |        3.29, 3.30 | 2.78, 2.68 |        16.95 | 13.32 |
| transaction(), two creates       |        2.72, 2.74 | 2.17, 2.14 |        13.46 | 10.22 |
| create, no transaction           |        0.89, 0.89 | 0.89, 0.89 |         3.85 |  3.81 |

The same over real HTTP, 16 clients, 6 s a case, two runs of each, requests a
second. Next door the gain is smaller: a request takes the server about 1.2 ms
of CPU, against a 0.57 ms round trip saved.

| Case           | Next door, before |      After | 2 ms, before |    After |
| -------------- | ----------------: | ---------: | -----------: | -------: |
| REST update    |          845, 917 |   955, 930 |     488, 493 | 573, 590 |
| GraphQL update |          857, 857 |   930, 890 |     487, 471 | 548, 593 |
| REST create    |        1431, 1404 | 1468, 1343 |      not run |  not run |

A create alone has no transaction, so it has nothing to gain. Faults on the new
code (a killed server, a terminated connection, a cut network, a failover, an
address that vanishes) end as before: back within the same seconds, nothing left
in flight, a stop under 30 ms. A soak of 5 minutes kept its heap flat at 99 MB.

Rejected for now: sending COMMIT with the last write as well. It saves another
round trip, but what runs after that write, a selected virtual field for one,
could no longer undo it.

## D-298: A quiet server keeps its connections

Choice: the pool keeps an idle connection for 5 minutes instead of the driver's
10 s, asks the system to probe it from 1 s of silence on, and does not hold the
process open for it. This reverses a reason D-287 gave for rejecting `keepAlive`:
that the pool closes idle connections within 10 s.

Opening a connection costs about ten reads: TCP, SCRAM, `set jit = off`, and the
statements prepared again. A server that gets a request every 15 s paid that on
every one of them, and every connection paid it after a pause.

1. `idleTimeoutMillis: 300_000`. Five minutes, not one: a pause of a few minutes
   is an ordinary pause on a small application. A longer one changes little for
   the server and holds the connections longer.
2. `keepAlive: true`, `keepAliveInitialDelayMillis: 1000`. Under Linux a socket
   whose peer vanished then fails by itself, and the pool drops it. A delay of
   10 s measured a window above 17 s.
3. `allowExitOnIdle: true`. Nothing else in the pool holds a script open now:
   without it, a script that forgets `stop()` would wait 5 minutes.

Measured, 4 runs of 11 s pauses, median in ms, no TLS:

| Case                              | Before | After |
| --------------------------------- | ------ | ----- |
| Next door, warm read              | 0.76   | 0.78  |
| Next door, first read after pause | 11.51  | 2.52  |
| Next door, 16 reads after pause   | 22.71  | 6.28  |
| 2 ms away, warm read              | 3.48   | 3.48  |
| 2 ms away, first read after pause | 22.00  | 5.11  |
| 2 ms away, 16 reads after pause   | 35.74  | 11.50 |

A script that forgets `stop()` ended 10.00 s after its last read, and now 0.00 s.

The database moving to another address without a word, no realtime, a read some
seconds after the connection's last use: it hangs until 8 s and answers from 12 s
before, it hangs until 12 s and answers from 14 s now. The read answers in 11 to
13 ms from there on, up to 62 s measured. So the blind window goes from about 10 s
to about 13 s. A statement sent inside it waits for the operating system, as it
did (D-287). A database restarted answers in 17 ms either way.

What this costs, and to whom:

- The server holds up to `connections` idle backends for 5 minutes, 1.5 MB each
  when fresh and 6 MB after 50 prepared statements. Several processes sharing a
  small `max_connections` overlap more than they did.
- A database that suspends when nobody is connected suspends up to 5 minutes later.
- A proxy that answers probes for a database gone silently hides it, which is why
  D-287 rejected this. An idle connection may then stay stale for 5 minutes and a
  statement sent on it hangs. Not tested through a proxy. With realtime, the
  listener still cuts it within about 30 s.
- A probe a second on each idle connection, about 114 MB a day at most for 10 of
  them, computed and not measured.

Rejected: a ping from the application when there is no realtime. It would cover
the proxy case by adding the timer D-287 keeps to the listener, for a limit a
public statement timeout would close more directly.

## D-299: Rows sharing a related row share its answer

Choice: when a flush asks which rows may pass a filter through a relation
(D-255, D-263), the rows that lead to the same related row get one answer. A
team's posts ask once whether the viewer is a member, not once per post.

Before, each row walked its related rows again: a write of 1000 documents across
50 teams asked each of 1000 lists the same 50 questions 20 times each. The
answer depends on the related row alone, so it is kept in a map for the pass,
keyed by the rows a relation holds for it; a many-to-one relation now gives the
same holding to the rows that name the same target.

Measured on `bench/realtime/teams.ts`: 1000 subscribers, 50 teams, 3 teams each,
50 000 documents, a window of 25; two passes of 12 writes, median in ms, from the
write's return.

| Rows written | Last message before | Last message after | Last statement before | Last statement after |
| -----------: | ------------------: | -----------------: | --------------------: | -------------------: |
|            1 |            8.9, 8.9 |           8.3, 8.8 |              5.2, 5.1 |             5.0, 5.5 |
|          100 |        112.9, 110.9 |       105.6, 103.3 |            45.6, 42.2 |           44.9, 45.0 |
|         1000 |        461.0, 456.5 |       281.8, 277.8 |          150.4, 191.7 |           87.3, 84.1 |

At 1000 rows the old pass ran long enough to split a flush: 1208 to 1242 messages
for 1000 lists, 1000 now. The statements are the same, 4 a write.

Two processes writing to one another's live lists through a membership rule,
12 rounds of 5 s, wrote 11 to 13 % more in all without a bulk update, 6 to 8 %
with one, which waits on its locks.

What this costs: one map per relation a pass walks, as many entries as related
rows. A row that leads to nothing shares an empty holding with the others.

## D-300: A row the flush's related rows refuse is read again from the store

Choice: when a flush refills a live list (D-288), a row it places that the
related rows the flush holds refuse (D-255, D-259) is read once more from the
store, without them, before it is counted as gone.

The flush reads the related rows when it starts; the refill reads the store
later, and may find a row that a write in between made readable, a membership
created since. Judged by the older related rows, that row was refused: it left
the window as gone, and after three refills the read failed with "The rows the
live plan finds are not readable" and read the whole list again.

Measured with two processes writing to one another's live lists through a
membership rule, 12 rounds of 5 s, two passes: the error fell from 6 and 5 a
run to 1 and 1, and the writes rose 5 % and 1 % in all, 14 % and 15 % over the
last three rounds, where the lists are longest. The error left comes from a
whole read outside a flush, a race of its own.

What this costs: one more read of the refused rows, only in a flush that holds
related rows and only when it refuses some.

## D-301: The type check builds the separate programs in one process

Amended by D-323.

Choice: amends D-173. `yarn typecheck` checks the root project, then the
starter's template, each with its own `tsc --project`, then generates the
website's sources, and builds every other program in one
`tsc --build --force`. Each example stays its own program, as an application
is. Nothing changes for a developer of an application.

Why: the 32 programs ran one after another, at about 1.4 s each, mostly a
start. One `tsc --build` runs them side by side in one process.

- `yarn typecheck`, three interleaved runs of each: 26.3, 26.7 and 26.6 s
  before, 15.9, 16.0 and 15.8 s after. That is about 11 of the 89 s of a warm
  `yarn validate`.
- `--build` checks the same programs. A wrong type in an example or a package
  still fails the run.
- `--force` builds every program on every run. These programs emit nothing,
  so `--build` has no output to compare, and a build info file must never be
  allowed to skip one.

The root project goes first and alone: an error in a package then shows once,
where `--build` would print it once for each program that reads the package.

The template stays out of `--build`, since `--build` writes a
`tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` beside each tsconfig. Git ignores that file, but
`yarn pack` would put the template's in the starter package, and the starter
copies the template as it is into every new application.

Rejected:

- Running the `tsc` commands 4 to 12 at a time with `xargs -P`: 17 s, since
  TypeScript 7 already uses several cores for each program.
- More builders with `--builders`: the same 13.5 to 14.5 s.
- Merging the examples into one program: each declares its own models, as an
  application does.

## D-302: An instance runs 20 runs at once

Choice: amends D-221, point 10. An instance runs at most 20 runs at once, the
runs its commits start and those its poll finds alike. A run waits for a place
in the order it started, and takes the place a run frees at once. The poll
reads the due rows 20 at a time, only once every run before them has a place,
and does not wait for them to end. When the instance stops, the runs still
waiting for a place are dropped: their rows stay due for the next instance.
A run that fails outside its job, as when the database is down, ends the
poll until the next one, and fails `runJobs()` with "runJobs could not run a
job.", the error as its cause. Nothing changes for a developer of an
application.

Why: a commit started its run at once, with no limit. 2000 runs enqueued at
once ran 2000 at once and held the pool's 10 connections: a read of the
application waited about half a second. The poll ran 20 rows and waited for
the slowest before it read the next 20, so one slow run held 19 places.

Measured on postgres, three interleaved runs of each, before and after:

- 2000 runs enqueued at once, each one read and 5 ms: at most 2000 runs at
  once before, 20 after. A read made meanwhile took 408 to 448 ms at the
  median before, 2.4 to 3.0 ms after; 1475 to 1654 ms at the 95th
  percentile before, 4.5 to 7.1 ms after. All 2000 ended in 2.9 to 3.2 s
  before, 3.05 to 3.5 s after.
- 1000 due rows, 20 of them 500 ms and the others 5 ms: 10.35 to 10.40 s
  through `runJobs()` before, 2.16 to 2.39 s after; 5.84 to 5.87 s through
  the poll before, 1.38 to 1.40 s after.

What it costs: work that only waits, as a slow call to another service, runs
20 at a time in each instance where it ran without a limit. A queue that
needs more runs on more instances.

Before, a failure outside a job was logged, and `runJobs()` passed with
nothing run: a test of a job then failed on what the job did, not on why.
The poll now reads the next rows without waiting for the runs before, so it
must stop on that failure, or it would read the same due rows again at once.

Rejected:

- An option for the number of places: nothing tells a developer what to set
  it to, as the poll's five seconds (D-221).
- A place for each connection of the pool: the pool is the adapter's, and a
  job may make no read at all.
- Running the waiting runs before the instance stops: 2000 waiting runs
  would hold the stop for as long as they take.

## D-303: `diskFiles()` writes an upload 1 MiB at a time

Choice: `diskFiles()` reads 16 chunks of an upload ahead, about 1 MiB as a
socket gives 64 KiB chunks, and writes its file through a 1 MiB buffer.
`s3()`, `memoryFiles()` and the upload route do not change. Nothing changes
for a developer of an application.

Why: it read one chunk ahead and wrote through Node's 16 KiB buffer, so the
socket waited on each write, and an upload reached half to two thirds of
what a bare `node:http` server writing the same body to disk reaches.

Measured with curl uploading to the HTTP plugin on the memory adapter,
`time_total` against a bare `node:http` server, three interleaved runs of
each, before and after: a 5 MB file 391 to 444 MB/s before, 525 to 560 MB/s
after; a 200 MB file 771 to 856 MB/s before, 1045 to 1100 MB/s after, the
bare server 1180 to 1330 MB/s. The download is unchanged, as near the bare
server as before.

What it costs: an upload holds up to about 2 MiB, read ahead and buffered,
only while the disk is slower than its client.

Rejected:

- Reading ahead in the upload route, for every storage: `s3()` gained
  nothing on SeaweedFS, which it sends to near its own rate, and would hold
  1 MiB more for each upload.
- Buffers of 64 KiB or 256 KiB: 384 to 452 and 443 to 465 MB/s on 5 MB,
  against 516 to 535 MB/s at 1 MiB.

## D-304: Unit tests share their modules within a worker

Choice: amends D-173. The `unit` project runs with `isolate: false`: a
